# Outcomes

Tools & Memory

- By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain why LLMs need a framework to hold a conversation, and what `create_agent`'s loop actually does.
- By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain what a tool is and what differentiates it from a plain Python function.
- By the end of this lesson, you will be able to build a custom tool to solve a problem and wire it into an agent.
- By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain what short-term memory is, and how it differs from long-term memory.

## Part 0 — The anatomy of `create_agent`

<!-- instructor: MVP delivery is verbal — walk through this out loud, no slides required. Land the key point: the loop that reads tool descriptions and decides what to call is code create_agent runs for you, not something the model provider does on its own. -->

A plain LLM call is stateless — it has no memory of anything outside the text you send it. If you wanted an agent that could hold a conversation and use tools on its own, you'd have to write that looping logic yourself: send a message, check if the model wants to call something, run it, send the result back, repeat.

`create_agent` does that looping for you. Today you'll see both halves of what it's doing under the hood: giving the agent something to call (a tool), and giving it something to remember (short-term memory).

---

## Problem 1 — Shelley wants to know if you have blue hoodies

<!-- instructor: run this live. The point is the agent can't know real inventory — it will guess, hedge, or hallucinate. Don't rescue it; let the wrong answer land. -->

Shelley messages your retail chatbot: *"Do you have the blue hoodie in stock?"* Your agent doesn't have access to your actual inventory. Try it and see what happens:

```python
%pip install -q -U langchain langchain-google-genai

import os
from google.colab import userdata
os.environ["GOOGLE_API_KEY"] = userdata.get("GOOGLE_API_KEY")

from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    tools=[],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful retail assistant.",
)

response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Do you have the blue hoodie in stock?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)
```

The agent has no way to actually know. It will guess, hedge, or make something up.

::: {.callout-note}
## Discuss
Why can't the agent answer this correctly on its own, no matter how the question is worded?
:::

### Give it real inventory access

Here's a function that checks real stock. It isn't a tool yet — fill in the three blanks to make it one:

```python
# FILL IN 1 — what decorator turns a plain function into a tool the agent can call?

def check_inventory(item: str, color: str = None) -> str:
    """FILL IN 2 — describe what this does and when the agent should use it"""
    fake_stock = {
        ("hoodie", "blue"): 4,
        ("hoodie", "black"): 12,
        ("t-shirt", "blue"): 30,
    }
    count = fake_stock.get((item.lower(), color.lower() if color else None), 0)
    label = f"{color} {item}" if color else item
    return f"We have {count} {label}(s) in stock." if count else f"We're out of {label} right now."

agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    tools=[],  # FILL IN 3 — add the tool here
    system_prompt="You are a helpful retail assistant.",
)
```

<!-- instructor: walk through filling these in together, but land on a deliberately weak docstring — "Handles inventory stuff." — so the next run misbehaves. Same "bad description" idea as the current lesson1_2.qmd's callout, now experienced instead of just read about. -->

Filled in together, it looks like this:

```python
@tool
def check_inventory(item: str, color: str = None) -> str:
    """Handles inventory stuff."""
    fake_stock = {
        ("hoodie", "blue"): 4,
        ("hoodie", "black"): 12,
        ("t-shirt", "blue"): 30,
    }
    count = fake_stock.get((item.lower(), color.lower() if color else None), 0)
    label = f"{color} {item}" if color else item
    return f"We have {count} {label}(s) in stock." if count else f"We're out of {label} right now."

agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    tools=[check_inventory],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful retail assistant.",
)

response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Do you have the blue hoodie in stock?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)
```

Run it. It still doesn't answer correctly — the docstring doesn't tell the agent *when* to use the tool or *what* it needs to call it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Discuss
What do you think went wrong — was the tool even called? How could you check?
:::

### Fix it

The function works fine. The description doesn't. Rewrite the docstring so the agent knows exactly when and how to use it:

```python
@tool
def check_inventory(item: str, color: str = None) -> str:
    """Check how many units of an item are in stock, optionally filtered by color.
    Use this whenever a customer asks whether an item is available or in stock."""
    fake_stock = {
        ("hoodie", "blue"): 4,
        ("hoodie", "black"): 12,
        ("t-shirt", "blue"): 30,
    }
    count = fake_stock.get((item.lower(), color.lower() if color else None), 0)
    label = f"{color} {item}" if color else item
    return f"We have {count} {label}(s) in stock." if count else f"We're out of {label} right now."

agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    tools=[check_inventory],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful retail assistant.",
)

response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Do you have the blue hoodie in stock?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)
```

Expected output: `We have 4 blue hoodie(s) in stock.` Now it works — because the docstring told the agent what the tool does and when to reach for it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Discuss
What actually changed between the two docstrings? Which words do you think mattered most?
:::

## Problem 2 — Shelley asks a follow-up

<!-- instructor: run this as a completely fresh invoke, no shared history, so the failure is guaranteed and visible. -->

Shelley isn't done: *"What about in black?"* Try it as a new question, same as before:

```python
response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What about in black?"}]})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)
```

The agent has no idea what "it" refers to — it never saw the word "hoodie" in this call. It might ask what item you mean, or guess wrong.

::: {.callout-note}
## Discuss
The tool worked fine a minute ago — so why does the agent suddenly seem to have forgotten everything?
:::

### What's missing

The model doesn't remember anything between calls. Each `agent.invoke()` starts from nothing unless *you* hand it the conversation so far. Fill in the blank below to carry the first exchange forward into the second:

```python
first_response = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Do you have the blue hoodie in stock?"}]})

messages = ____  # FILL IN — how do we carry the conversation so far into the next call?
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "What about in black?"})

second_response = agent.invoke({"messages": messages})
print(second_response["messages"][-1].content)
```

<!-- instructor: blank is `first_response["messages"]`. Emphasize this is a list they're building up themselves — the mechanism, not magic. -->

Filled in: `messages = first_response["messages"]`. Run it now.

Expected output: `We have 12 black hoodie(s) in stock.` This time it resolves "it" correctly, because the whole conversation — not just the latest question — went into the call.

::: {.callout-note}
## Discuss
Where does "memory" actually live here — in the model, in `create_agent`, or in your own code? What would happen if you forgot to include `first_response["messages"]`?
:::

## Apply It — a fresh problem, on your own

<!-- instructor: independent practice, no blanks. Supply Chain use case, combining both pieces from scratch in a new context. -->

A customer messages your shipping company: *"Where is shipment TRK-4821?"* Your agent doesn't have shipment data yet, and after it answers, the customer will ask a follow-up ("Has it left the warehouse yet?") that only makes sense if the agent remembers the tracking ID.

Build this yourself, start to finish:

1. Write a `get_shipment_status(tracking_id: str) -> str` tool with a clear docstring, using fake data of your own
2. Wire it into an agent and confirm the first question gets answered correctly
3. Ask the follow-up question, carrying the conversation forward the same way you just did for Shelley
4. Confirm the agent correctly resolves what "it" refers to *and* calls the tool again to answer

::: {.callout-important}
